title: Data-driven initiatives to assess climate risks, provide solutions - Deccan Herald
full_text:
Bengaluru: Research organisations showcased models that can help the governments in making decisions to prevent damage to life and extreme weather events associated with global warming and climate change, at an event to mark Climate Week in Bengaluru on Monday.
The Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (CSTEP) has come up with BHRIGU, a platform that seeks to bridge gaps in data to provide insights for policy and action on hazards like heatwave and floods.
The project, Building Heat Resilience in India’s Growing Urbanscapes (BHRIGU), seeks to build resilience in Indian cities expected to host 60 crore people by 2036. The project will work across six representative urban landscapes to co-develop risk assessment tools and embed climate resilience into planning and governance.
In a parallel event, World Resources Institute launched Data Lab Connect, an initiative that seeks to provide solutions to organisations working on similar challenges, from urban heat stress to changing water trends. The platform relies on data and analytical approaches to assess risks and vulnerabilities at local level.

title: Karnataka coffee output may fall 15 to 20% in 2026-27, planters warn. How is El Nino hitting the crop? - Moneycontrol.com
full_text:
Coffee production in Karnataka, which accounts for around 70% of India’s output, could drop 15 to 20% in 2026-27 as rising temperatures, erratic rain and prolonged dry spells threaten plantations even as super El Nino conditions intensify over the Indian subcontinent, TOI reported.
The Karnataka Planters Association (KPA) has warned of this sharper contraction, while the United Planters’ Association of South India (UPASI) expects a smaller fall of 7 to 10% across south India and the Northeast. The projections come against the Coffee Board’s post-blossom estimate of 4 lakh metric tonnes (MT) for the country this year, up from the final output of 3.7 lakh MT in 2025-26, the report said.
KPA president Salman Baseer said Karnataka’s post-blossom estimate stands at 2.8 lakh MT, made up of 84,015 MT of Arabica and 1.9 lakh MT of Robusta, as per the report. The final output last year was 2.6 lakh MT. He said the drought conditions were likely to push production down by 15 to 20%, calling it a severe setback for the state’s plantation economy, and added that the KPA had appealed to the state and central governments to step in and help the sector through the crisis.
UPASI’s estimates put Arabica output at around one lakh MT, against the Coffee Board’s projection of 1.2 lakh MT, as per the report. It added that Robusta production is also expected to fall from the board’s estimate of 2.8 lakh MT.
The damage may not end with this harvest, according to Sahadev Balakrishna, chairperson of UPASI’s Coffee Committee. He was cited as saying that the crisis may not fully unfold in 2026, since some erratic rain was received in August and September and the forecast points to a near-normal northeast monsoon.
The real danger, Balakrishna said, lies beyond this year’s crop. If the heat stress continues alongside long dry spells in early 2027, productivity could suffer and the extent of the damage will depend on the duration and intensity of the stress, the recovery in rainfall and the condition of the plantations.
Office-bearers of both associations, speaking ahead of the KPA’s 68th annual general body meeting in Chikkamagaluru on Monday, indicated that coffee prices in the Indian and global markets are unlikely to see significant volatility in 2026-27, the report noted. KPA office-bearers said the coming months would be crucial in determining the extent of the damage.
